source: During gastrulation epiblast cells exit pluripotency as they specify and spatially arrange the three germ layers of the embryo.

claim: Human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) undergo spatially organized fate specification on micropatterned surfaces.
source: Similarly, human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) undergo spatially organized fate specification on micropatterned surfaces.
evidence: This statement references prior work on human PSCs and micropatterning.

claim: A mouse PSC micropattern system was developed.
source: we developed a mouse PSC micropattern system
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript describing the development of a new system.

claim: The mouse PSC micropattern system reveals robust specification of distinct regional identities with direct comparisons to mouse embryos.
source: we developed a mouse PSC micropattern system and, with direct comparisons to mouse embryos, reveal the robust specification of distinct regional identities.

claim: BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF directed mouse epiblast-like cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF directed mouse epiblast-like cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and radially pattern posterior mesoderm fates.

claim: BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF directed mouse epiblast-like cells to radially pattern posterior mesoderm fates.
source: BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF directed mouse epiblast-like cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and radially pattern posterior mesoderm fates.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF patterned anterior identities, including definitive endoderm.
source: Conversely, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF patterned anterior identities, including definitive endoderm.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Epiblast stem cells, a developmentally advanced state, only specified anterior identities, but without patterning.
source: By contrast, epiblast stem cells, a developmentally advanced state, only specified anterior identities, but without patterning.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding comparing different pluripotent cell states.

claim: Gastrulation is the process of coordinated cell fate specification, spatial patterning and morphogenesis that establishes the blueprint of the adult organism.
source: Gastrulation is the process of coordinated cell fate specification, spatial patterning and morphogenesis that establishes the blueprint of the adult organism.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: During gastrulation, the pluripotent epiblast (Epi) differentiates into the three definitive germ layers of the embryo; the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
source: During gastrulation, the pluripotent epiblast (Epi) differentiates into the three definitive germ layers of the embryo; the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: In the mouse, gastrulation events are initiated at approximately embryonic day (E) 6.25 by a convergence of signals, emanating from both extraembryonic and embryonic tissues, acting at the proximal, posterior of the embryo.
source: In the mouse, these events are initiated at approximately embryonic day (E) 6.25 by a convergence of signals, emanating from both extraembryonic and embryonic tissues, acting at the proximal, posterior of the embryo.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about mouse development.

claim: The BMP/Wnt/Nodal/FGF signaling hub drives posterior Epi cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: The resulting BMP/Wnt/Nodal/FGF signaling hub drives posterior Epi cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Hashimoto and Nakatsuji, 1989; Tam and Loebel, 2007; Arnold and Robertson, 2009), establishing a dynamic territory referred to as the primitive streak (PS).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The BMP/Wnt/Nodal/FGF signaling hub establishes a dynamic territory referred to as the primitive streak (PS).
source: The resulting BMP/Wnt/Nodal/FGF signaling hub drives posterior Epi cells to undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Hashimoto and Nakatsuji, 1989; Tam and Loebel, 2007; Arnold and Robertson, 2009), establishing a dynamic territory referred to as the primitive streak (PS).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PS elongates and extends distally as gastrulation proceeds.
source: The PS elongates and extends distally as gastrulation proceeds.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Distinct cell types are specified depending on the time and position at which they undergo EMT and exit the PS.
source: Distinct cell types are specified depending on the time and position at which they undergo EMT and exit the PS (Kinder et al., 1999; Lawson, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Emerging mesenchymal cells either move proximally and laterally, forming the extraembryonic mesoderm, or bilaterally in an anterior direction circumnavigating the space between the Epi and outer visceral endoderm (VE) layers, giving rise to the embryonic mesoderm and definitive endoderm (DE).
source: Emerging mesenchymal cells either move proximally and laterally, forming the extraembryonic mesoderm, or bilaterally in an anterior direction circumnavigating the space between the Epi and outer visceral endoderm (VE) layers, giving rise to the embryonic mesoderm and definitive endoderm (DE).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about cell movements during gastrulation.

claim: Epi cells that maintain an epithelial state and do not ingress through the PS form the ectoderm.
source: Epi cells that maintain an epithelial state and do not ingress through the PS form the ectoderm.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) are the in vitro counterpart of the pluripotent Epi of the embryo.
source: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) are the in vitro counterpart of the pluripotent Epi of the embryo.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PSCs.

claim: PSCs can be expanded indefinitely and differentiated into derivatives of all germ layers.
source: They can be expanded indefinitely and differentiated into derivatives of all germ layers (Keller, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Standard differentiation protocols generate cell fates in a spatially disorganized manner that is incomparable with in vivo gastrulation.
source: Standard differentiation protocols generate cell fates in a spatially disorganized manner that is incomparable with in vivo gastrulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of standard protocols, based on established knowledge.

claim: When human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) were differentiated within geometrically uniform, circular micropatterns, they reproducibly patterned cell fates with radial symmetry.
source: However, it was recently it was shown that, when human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) were differentiated within geometrically uniform, circular micropatterns, they reproducibly patterned cell fates with radial symmetry (Warmflash et al., 2014; Tewary et al., 2017; Etoc et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on hESCs.

claim: hESC micropatterned colonies were suggested to give rise to a central ectoderm population followed by concentric circular territories of mesoderm, endoderm, and an outer trophectoderm layer.
source: Based on a limited number of markers, hESC micropatterned colonies were suggested to give rise to a central ectoderm population followed by concentric circular territories of mesoderm, endoderm, and an outer trophectoderm layer (Warmflash et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on hESCs.

claim: The hESC micropattern findings revealed the capacity of the BMP, Wnt and Nodal signaling pathways to collectively organize cell fates.
source: These findings revealed the capacity of the BMP, Wnt and Nodal signaling pathways to collectively organize cell fates.
evidence: This statement is an interpretation of prior work on hESCs.

claim: The micropattern system is scalable and reproducible.
source: The scalability and reproducibility of this assay coupled with the ease of genetically modifying PSCs, the ability to manipulate culture conditions and the simplicity of imaging make this a robust and attractive system to disentangle the cellular behaviors and signaling interactions that pattern mammalian embryos.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the micropattern system.

claim: The human organotypic micropattern system raised many questions, largely due to the absence of a human in vivo standard for direct comparison and assignment of cell identities.
source: Even so, this human organotypic system raised many questions, largely due to the absence of a human in vivo standard for direct comparison and assignment of cell identities.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the human system.

claim: The micropattern-based system was adapted to defined medium conditions to precisely dissect signaling requirements.
source: Here we adapted the micropattern-based system to defined medium conditions to precisely dissect signaling requirements, and to mouse PSCs for which in vivo reference points are accessible to assign cell fates.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The micropattern-based system was adapted to mouse PSCs for which in vivo reference points are accessible to assign cell fates.
source: Here we adapted the micropattern-based system to defined medium conditions to precisely dissect signaling requirements, and to mouse PSCs for which in vivo reference points are accessible to assign cell fates.
evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: Mouse ESCs were first converted to epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), the in vitro counterpart of the Epi of the early pre-gastrulation embryo.
source: We first converted mouse ESCs to epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs), the in vitro counterpart of the Epi of the early pre-gastrulation embryo (Hayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work defining EpiLCs.

claim: Mouse EpiLCs seeded onto circular micropatterned surfaces formed a simple epithelial morphology in a flat-disc geometry.
source: Mouse EpiLCs seeded onto circular micropatterned surfaces formed a simple epithelial morphology in a flat-disc geometry.
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation.

claim: By all markers examined, micropatterned EpiLCs were identical to the Epi of the E5.5-E6.0 embryo.
source: By all markers examined, these cells were identical to the Epi of the E5.5-E6.0 embryo.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on marker analysis comparing in vitro and in vivo cells.

claim: When exposed to gastrulation-promoting factors, micropatterned EpiLCs underwent an EMT and recapitulated organized germ layer differentiation of specific regions of the mouse gastrula.
source: When exposed to gastrulation-promoting factors, micropatterned EpiLCs underwent an EMT and recapitulated organized germ layer differentiation of specific regions of the mouse gastrula.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The cup-shaped geometry of the rodent embryo is not requisite for the spatial patterning of mouse pluripotent cells.
source: This demonstrated that the cup-shaped geometry of the rodent embryo is not requisite for the spatial patterning of mouse pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing patterning in flat-disc geometry.

claim: The capacity to undergo spatially organized germ layer differentiation under these conditions was specific to EpiLCs.
source: Furthermore, the capacity to undergo spatially organized germ layer differentiation under these conditions was specific to EpiLCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing different pluripotent cell states.

claim: Under the same conditions neither ESCs, corresponding the pre-implantation Epi, nor epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), corresponding to the gastrulating Epi, demonstrated robust cell fate patterning.
source: Under the same conditions neither ESCs, corresponding the pre-implantation Epi, nor epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), corresponding to the gastrulating Epi (Figure 1A), demonstrated robust cell fate patterning.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing different pluripotent cell states.

claim: A proximal-to-distal gradient of BMP signaling activity was observed in vivo, with cells in the posterior (proximal) PS exhibiting high signaling activity, while those in the anterior (distal) PS showed no activity.
source: In vivo, we observed a proximal-to-distal gradient of BMP signaling activity – cells in the posterior (proximal) PS exhibited high signaling activity, while those in the anterior (distal) PS showed no activity.
evidence: This is a primary observation from in vivo embryo analysis.

claim: Exposure of micropatterned EpiLCs to posterior signals, BMP, FGF, ACTIVIN (NODAL) and WNT, promoted an EMT and acquisition of posterior Epi, PS, embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm identities.
source: Exposure of micropatterned EpiLCs to posterior signals, BMP, FGF, ACTIVIN (NODAL) and WNT, promoted an EMT and acquisition of posterior Epi, PS, embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm identities.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: When BMP was removed, emulating the anterior PS environment (in which FGF, ACTIVIN and WNT are acting), anterior Epi, anterior PS and/or AxM and DE cell types were formed.
source: When BMP was removed, emulating the anterior PS environment (in which FGF, ACTIVIN and WNT are acting), anterior Epi, anterior PS and/or AxM and DE cell types were formed.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: In vitro micropattern differentiation parallels events occurring during gastrulation in vivo in mammalian embryos.
source: Hence, we demonstrated for the first time that in vitro micropattern differentiation parallels events occurring during gastrulation in vivo in mammalian embryos, and that mouse PSCs residing in a flat-disc geometry can pattern cohorts of neighboring regional identities correlating with those established in the embryo.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: Mouse PSCs residing in a flat-disc geometry can pattern cohorts of neighboring regional identities correlating with those established in the embryo.
source: Hence, we demonstrated for the first time that in vitro micropattern differentiation parallels events occurring during gastrulation in vivo in mammalian embryos, and that mouse PSCs residing in a flat-disc geometry can pattern cohorts of neighboring regional identities correlating with those established in the embryo.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: BMP4 is directly required for posterior mesoderm formation.
source: We established a direct requirement for BMP4 in posterior mesoderm formation, and demonstrated that BMP signaling is not required for DE and anterior PS/AxM specification.
evidence: This is a primary finding from manipulating BMP signaling in the micropattern system.

claim: BMP signaling is not required for DE and anterior PS/AxM specification.
source: We established a direct requirement for BMP4 in posterior mesoderm formation, and demonstrated that BMP signaling is not required for DE and anterior PS/AxM specification.
evidence: This is a primary finding from manipulating BMP signaling in the micropattern system.

claim: Prior to the onset of gastrulation (E5.5-E6.0), the Epi is in a formative state of pluripotency whereby naïve pre-implantation markers have been downregulated but differentiation has not yet commenced.
source: Prior to the onset of gastrulation (E5.5-E6.0), the Epi is in a formative state of pluripotency whereby naïve pre-implantation markers, present in the blastocyst, have been downregulated but differentiation has not yet commenced (Figure 1B) (Morgani et al., 2017; Smith, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and Figure 1B showing marker expression.

claim: Global transcriptional profiling identified EpiLCs as the closest in vitro counterpart of the formative Epi.
source: Global transcriptional profiling identified EpiLCs as the closest in vitro counterpart of the formative Epi (Hayashi et al., 2011; Smith, 2017; Kalkan et al., 2017; Kalkan and Smith, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior transcriptional profiling studies.

claim: Fibronectin and Laminin are basement membrane components present at the Epi-VE interface of peri-gastrulation mouse embryos.
source: Fibronectin and Laminin are basement membrane components present at the Epi-VE interface of peri-gastrulation mouse embryos (Viotti et al., 2014; Bedzhov and Zernicka-Goetz, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EpiLCs are generated on a Fibronectin substrate.
source: While EpiLCs are generated on a Fibronectin substrate (Hayashi et al., 2011), we noted superior adhesion of cells to the micropatterns when coating them with Laminin.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the EpiLC generation protocol.

claim: Superior adhesion of cells to the micropatterns was noted when coating them with Laminin.
source: While EpiLCs are generated on a Fibronectin substrate (Hayashi et al., 2011), we noted superior adhesion of cells to the micropatterns when coating them with Laminin.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Micropatterned EpiLCs expressed the pluripotency-associated markers POU5F1 (OCT4), SOX2, NANOG and OTX2.
source: Like the pre-streak Epi, micropatterned EpiLCs expressed the pluripotency-associated markers POU5F1 (OCT4), SOX2, NANOG and OTX2, as well as the post-implantation Epi marker, POU3F1 (OCT6) (Figure 1B,D) (Zhu et al., 2014; Acampora et al., 2013; Avilion et al., 2003; Rosner et al., 1990; Hart et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B,D showing marker expression and citations.

claim: Micropatterned EpiLCs expressed the post-implantation Epi marker, POU3F1 (OCT6).
source: Like the pre-streak Epi, micropatterned EpiLCs expressed the pluripotency-associated markers POU5F1 (OCT4), SOX2, NANOG and OTX2, as well as the post-implantation Epi marker, POU3F1 (OCT6) (Figure 1B,D) (Zhu et al., 2014; Acampora et al., 2013; Avilion et al., 2003; Rosner et al., 1990; Hart et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B,D showing marker expression and citations.

claim: Neither the Epi of the pre-gastrula embryo nor EpiLCs expressed KLF4, a key regulator of naïve pluripotency.
source: Neither the Epi of the pre-gastrula embryo nor EpiLCs expressed KLF4, a key regulator of naïve pluripotency (Figure 1B,D) (Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B,D showing absence of KLF4 and a citation.

claim: The pre-streak Epi does not express lineage-associated markers such as GATA6, FOXA2, CDX2 or BRACHYURY.
source: The pre-streak Epi does not express lineage-associated markers such as GATA6, FOXA2, CDX2 or BRACHYURY and, these were also absent from EpiLC colonies (Figure 1B,D) except in rare cells that we interpret as having spontaneously differentiated.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B,D showing absence of these markers.

claim: Lineage-associated markers such as GATA6, FOXA2, CDX2 or BRACHYURY were absent from EpiLC colonies except in rare cells that were interpreted as having spontaneously differentiated.
source: The pre-streak Epi does not express lineage-associated markers such as GATA6, FOXA2, CDX2 or BRACHYURY and, these were also absent from EpiLC colonies (Figure 1B,D) except in rare cells that we interpret as having spontaneously differentiated.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B,D and represents an interpretation of rare cells.

claim: Micropatterned EpiLC colonies formed an epithelial monolayer marked by CDH1 (E-CADHERIN).
source: Micropatterned EpiLC colonies formed an epithelial monolayer (marked by CDH1, also referred to as E-CADHERIN) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing CDH1 expression.

claim: Cell density within the EpiLC epithelium increased by nearly a factor of four in 24 hr.
source: Cell density within the epithelium increased by nearly a factor of four in 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Micropatterned EpiLCs exhibited a slightly lower cell density than the epithelium of the embryonic Epi at pre- and early gastrulation stages.
source: We noted that micropatterned EpiLCs exhibited a slightly lower cell density than the epithelium of the embryonic Epi at pre- and early gastrulation stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In vivo development can proceed when the Epi cell density is experimentally decreased.
source: However, in vivo development can also proceed when the Epi cell density is experimentally decreased (Kojima et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Micropatterned EpiLC colonies were spatially homogeneous.
source: Such quantification indicated that micropatterned EpiLC colonies were spatially homogeneous (Figure 1F), hence we started with a defined population correlating to the pre-gastrulation Epi at approximately E5.5-E6.0.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At the onset of gastrulation (E6.25-E6.75), SOX2 is elevated within the anterior Epi.
source: At the onset of gastrulation (E6.25-E6.75), the anterior and posterior of the Epi can be distinguished by the expression of specific markers. SOX2 is elevated within the anterior Epi, while NANOG is restricted to the posterior Epi (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Avilion et al., 2003; Hart et al., 2004; Morkel et al., 2003; Osorno et al., 2012; Di-Gregorio et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: At the onset of gastrulation (E6.25-E6.75), NANOG is restricted to the posterior Epi.
source: At the onset of gastrulation (E6.25-E6.75), the anterior and posterior of the Epi can be distinguished by the expression of specific markers. SOX2 is elevated within the anterior Epi, while NANOG is restricted to the posterior Epi (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Avilion et al., 2003; Hart et al., 2004; Morkel et al., 2003; Osorno et al., 2012; Di-Gregorio et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: The PS emerges in the proximal posterior Epi and is marked by BRACHYURY expression.
source: The PS emerges in the proximal posterior Epi and is marked by BRACHYURY expression (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Wilkinson et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and a citation.

claim: When micropatterned EpiLC colonies were cultured with FGF2 and ACTIVIN A for 72 hr, BRACHYURY was induced at the colony periphery.
source: When micropatterned EpiLC colonies were cultured with FGF2 and ACTIVIN A for 72 hr, BRACHYURY was induced at the colony periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D), reminiscent of PS formation.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: In the presence of a small molecule inhibitor of Wnt signaling, XAV939, BRACHYURY expression was abolished and SOX2 was homogeneously expressed at high levels.
source: In the presence of a small molecule inhibitor of Wnt signaling, XAV939 (Huang et al., 2009), BRACHYURY expression was abolished and SOX2 was homogeneously expressed at high levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D and a citation for XAV939.

claim: BMP inhibition had no obvious effect on BRACHYURY expression.
source: BMP inhibition had no obvious effect on BRACHYURY (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data is not shown.

claim: In micropatterned colonies, BRACHYURY expression was dependent on endogenous Wnt signaling.
source: Hence in micropatterned colonies, as in EpiSC cultures (Kim et al., 2013; Kurek et al., 2015; Tsakiridis et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2015; Sumi et al., 2013), BRACHYURY expression was dependent on endogenous Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the XAV939 experiment and citations to prior work in EpiSC cultures.

claim: FGF and ACTIVIN support a SOX2-high anterior Epi-like state.
source: This suggested that FGF and ACTIVIN support a SOX2-high anterior Epi-like state, while FGF and ACTIVIN combined with endogenous WNT trigger a reduction in SOX2 levels, as in the posterior Epi, and PS gene expression at the colony periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Table 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Table 1.

claim: FGF and ACTIVIN combined with endogenous WNT trigger a reduction in SOX2 levels, as in the posterior Epi, and PS gene expression at the colony periphery.
source: This suggested that FGF and ACTIVIN support a SOX2-high anterior Epi-like state, while FGF and ACTIVIN combined with endogenous WNT trigger a reduction in SOX2 levels, as in the posterior Epi, and PS gene expression at the colony periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Table 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Table 1.

claim: The later germ layer markers GATA6, SOX17 and CDX2 were not expressed under FGF, ACTIVIN and endogenous WNT conditions.
source: The later germ layer markers GATA6, SOX17 and CDX2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) were not expressed under these conditions indicating that additional factors were required to stimulate further differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Additional factors were required to stimulate further differentiation beyond the PS-like state.
source: The later germ layer markers GATA6, SOX17 and CDX2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) were not expressed under these conditions indicating that additional factors were required to stimulate further differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference from the absence of later markers.

claim: In vivo, gastrulation is triggered by a combination of signals from both embryonic Epi cells and the extraembryonic tissues that lie adjacent to the proximal posterior Epi.
source: In vivo, gastrulation is triggered by a combination of signals from both embryonic Epi cells and the extraembryonic tissues that lie adjacent to the proximal posterior Epi. The extraembryonic signals include WNT3 produced by the VE, and BMP4 produced by the extraembryonic ectoderm (ExE) (Tam and Loebel, 2007; Robertson, 2014) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 2D.

claim: The extraembryonic signals include WNT3 produced by the VE, and BMP4 produced by the extraembryonic ectoderm (ExE).
source: In vivo, gastrulation is triggered by a combination of signals from both embryonic Epi cells and the extraembryonic tissues that lie adjacent to the proximal posterior Epi. The extraembryonic signals include WNT3 produced by the VE, and BMP4 produced by the extraembryonic ectoderm (ExE) (Tam and Loebel, 2007; Robertson, 2014) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 2D.

claim: The mouse micropattern system likely lacked the neighboring extraembryonic cell types and the signals that they provide.
source: For the mouse micropattern differentiation we utilized pluripotent EpiLCs, corresponding to the Epi cells of the embryo, and thus the system likely lacked the neighboring extraembryonic cell types and the signals that they provide.
evidence: This is an inference about the composition of the in vitro system.

claim: After 24 hr of differentiation with exogenous BMP and WNT, EpiLC micropatterned colonies gave rise to a central population expressing the Epi markers POU5F1, SOX2 and NANOG, and an outer population expressing the PS marker BRACHYURY.
source: After 24 hr of differentiation, the EpiLC micropatterned colonies gave rise to two populations – a central population expressing the Epi markers POU5F1, SOX2 and NANOG, and an outer population expressing the PS marker BRACHYURY (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F,G showing marker expression.

claim: From 0 to 24 hr, SOX2 levels were reduced approximately 2-fold within the central population.
source: From 0 to 24 hr, SOX2 levels were reduced approximately 2-fold within the central population (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2F–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There was no change in NANOG expression from 0 to 24 hr.
source: Conversely, there was no change in NANOG expression (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A NANOG-positive, SOX2-low state emerged as is present in the posterior Epi of the embryo.
source: Hence, a NANOG-positive, SOX2-low state emerged as is present in the posterior Epi of the embryo (Hoffman et al., 2013) (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and a citation.

claim: BRACHYURY and SOX2 expression was predominantly mutually exclusive but showed a degree of overlap.
source: BRACHYURY and SOX2 expression was predominantly mutually exclusive but showed a degree of overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), which was also observed in cells within the PS in vivo (Figure 2A) and may mark an Epi-PS transition state.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and Figure 2A.

claim: At 24 hr, no later germ layer-associated markers (GATA6, SOX17, CDX2, FOXA2) were expressed.
source: At this time, no later germ layer-associated markers (GATA6, SOX17, CDX2, FOXA2) were expressed (Figure 2F,H).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F,H showing absence of these markers.

claim: The first 24 hr of micropattern differentiation with exogenous BMP and WNT generated populations resembling the posterior Epi and emerging PS of the mouse embryo at approximately E6.25-E6.75.
source: Hence, the first 24 hr of micropattern differentiation with exogenous BMP and WNT generated populations resembling the posterior Epi and emerging PS of the mouse embryo at approximately E6.25-E6.75, as observed in the presence of FGF, ACTIVIN and endogenous WNT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the marker analysis and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: At both 48 and 72 hr, the colony center continued to express NANOG and low levels of POU5F1 and SOX2 as in the posterior Epi.
source: At both 48 and 72 hr, the colony center continued to express NANOG and low levels of POU5F1 and SOX2 as in the posterior Epi (Figure 2F–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: At 72 hr, OTX2 and FOXA2 were observed within the colony center.
source: Additionally, at 72 hr, OTX2 and FOXA2 were observed within the colony center (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) analogous to the expression of these markers within the mid to distal region of the posterior Epi at E7.0-E7.5 (Figure 3A) (Engert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: The central population at 72 hr likely correlated to the posterior Epi later than E7.0, but prior to E7.75.
source: Therefore, based on the expression of FOXA2 but not CDX2, the central population likely correlated to the posterior Epi later than E7.0, but prior to E7.75.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns.

claim: At 48 and 72 hr BRACHYURY-positive cells were observed more centrally, within the mid micropattern domain.
source: However, at 48 and 72 hr BRACHYURY-positive cells were observed more centrally, within the mid micropattern domain (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F–H showing BRACHYURY distribution.

claim: The inwards shift of BRACHYURY suggested either a wave of gene expression propagating throughout the colony or an inward movement of BRACHYURY-expressing cells.
source: This inwards shift of BRACHYURY suggested either a wave of gene expression propagating throughout the colony or an inward movement of BRACHYURY-expressing cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed pattern.

claim: The majority of BRACHYURY-positive cells did not express GATA6 or CDX2/SOX17, and hence likely corresponded to PS.
source: While we observed cells that coexpressed BRACHYURY and GATA6 or CDX2/SOX17 (discussed later), the majority of BRACHYURY-positive cells did not express these markers, and hence likely corresponded to PS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: A small fraction of cells coexpressed GATA6 and BRACHYURY, as in the first cells leaving the PS.
source: A small fraction of cells coexpressed GATA6 and BRACHYURY, as in the first cells leaving the PS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,J,K).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,J,K.

claim: Cells that coexpressed GATA6 and OTX2 were observed, as in Mesoderm 1.
source: Additionally, we observed cells that coexpressed GATA6 and OTX2, as in Mesoderm 1 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,G).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,G.

claim: Mesoderm 2 was likely not generated under these in vitro differentiation conditions.
source: While in vivo we could also discern a second population of embryonic mesoderm (Mesoderm 2) that expressed FOXF1 and BRACHYURY (Figure 3B–D), within the micropatterned colonies FOXF1 was restricted to the colony periphery in a spatially distinct domain from BRACHYURY (Figures 2H and 3H). Hence Mesoderm 2 was likely not generated under these in vitro differentiation conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of markers shown in Figures 2H and 3H.

claim: At 48 hr, almost all CDX2-positive cells coexpressed BRACHYURY and SOX17.
source: At this time, almost all CDX2-positive cells coexpressed BRACHYURY and SOX17 (Figures 2F and 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figures 2F, 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BRACHYURY/SOX17/CDX2-positive cells correlated most strongly to the extraembryonic mesoderm ACD.
source: In vivo, coexpression of BRACHYURY, SOX17 and CDX2 is first observed within extraembryonic mesoderm cells of the ACD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). While BRACHYURY, SOX17 and CDX2 are also all expressed within cells of the hindgut at later stages of development (E8.5) (Lewis and Tam, 2006), this micropattern population did not express additional hindgut markers such as FOXA2 (Monaghan et al., 1993; Ang et al., 1993; Ruiz i Altaba et al., 1993) (Figure 3E). Hence BRACHYURY/SOX17/CDX2-positive cells correlated most strongly to the extraembryonic mesoderm ACD.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns and citations, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Figure 3E.

claim: At 72 hr, the BRACHYURY/SOX17/CDX2 population was no longer observed.
source: At 72 hr, the BRACHYURY/SOX17/CDX2 population was no longer observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: At 72 hr, SOX17/CDX2/FOXF1-positive cells likely corresponded to the AOM.
source: At 72 hr, CDX2-positive cells also expressed FOXF1, another marker found within the extraembryonic mesoderm (Figure 3D). Hence, SOX17/CDX2/FOXF1-positive cells likely corresponded to the AOM, suggesting a temporal progression of ACD cells to an AOM state, as in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: A temporal progression of ACD cells to an AOM state occurs, as in vivo.
source: Hence, SOX17/CDX2/FOXF1-positive cells likely corresponded to the AOM, suggesting a temporal progression of ACD cells to an AOM state, as in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal changes in marker expression.

claim: A rarer population of cells that coexpressed FOXF1 and GATA6 was observed, as in the YSM or embryonic mesoderm positioned between Mesoderm 1 and 2.
source: We also observed a rarer population of cells that coexpressed FOXF1 and GATA6 (Figure 3H, yellow arrowhead) as in the YSM or embryonic mesoderm positioned between Mesoderm 1 and 2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3H and Figure 3D.

claim: Both embryonic (GATA6) and extraembryonic (SOX17/CDX2/FOXF1) mesoderm-like populations were present within the outer micropattern domain and tended to exist within discrete clusters.
source: While both embryonic (GATA6) and extraembryonic (SOX17/CDX2/FOXF1) mesoderm-like populations were present within the outer micropattern domain, they tended to exist within discrete clusters (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3G.

claim: In the micropattern differentiation FOXA2, SOX17 and GATA6 were expressed in a mostly mutually exclusive manner, hence they marked separate non-DE populations.
source: In vivo these markers are coexpressed within DE cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) while in the micropattern differentiation FOXA2, SOX17 and GATA6 were expressed in a mostly mutually exclusive manner (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), hence they marked separate non-DE populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns, supported by Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BRACHYURY and FOXA2 were expressed within distinct micropattern domains (mid and central respectively) suggesting that AxM cells were not present.
source: Furthermore, BRACHYURY and FOXA2 were expressed within distinct micropattern domains (mid and central respectively) (Figures 2F,G and 3E) suggesting that AxM cells were not present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of markers, supported by Figures 2F,G and 3E.

claim: After 72 hr of differentiation, HhexRedStar was observed at the outer colony edge but GscGFP was not expressed.
source: After 72 hr of differentiation, HhexRedStar was observed at the outer colony edge but GscGFP was not expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2B showing reporter expression.

claim: The expression of HhexRedStar and SOX17, without FOXA2 and GscGFP expression, confirmed the absence of DE and AxM fates and likely indicated the presence of hematopoietic progenitors that arise from the allantois.
source: The expression of HhexRedStar and SOX17, without FOXA2 and GscGFP expression, confirmed the absence of DE and AxM fates and likely indicated the presence of hematopoietic progenitors that arise from the allantois (Thomas et al., 1998; Crompton et al., 1992)
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns and citations.

claim: In vitro, a combination of BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN (NODAL), and FGF promoted the specification and spatial organization of posterior Epi (center), PS (mid) and embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm (outer), recapitulating gastrulation events occurring within the posterior of the mouse gastrula.
source: Therefore, in vitro, a combination of BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN (NODAL), and FGF promoted the specification and spatial organization of posterior Epi (center), PS (mid) and embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm (outer), recapitulating gastrulation events occurring within the posterior of the mouse gastrula (Figure 3I, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the data and summarized in Figure 3I and Table 1.

claim: Fates arising from the anterior PS including DE and AxM were not formed under BMP, WNT, ACTIVIN and FGF conditions.
source: However, fates arising from the anterior PS including DE and AxM were not formed under these conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the marker analysis.

claim: One of the primary hallmarks of gastrulation is an EMT, involving downregulation of the epithelial marker CDH1 (E-CADHERIN) and upregulation of the mesenchymal marker CDH2 (N-CADHERIN) in cells ingressing through the PS.
source: One of the primary hallmarks of gastrulation is an EMT, involving downregulation of the epithelial marker CDH1 (E-CADHERIN) and upregulation of the mesenchymal marker CDH2 (N-CADHERIN) in cells ingressing through the PS (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge, supported by Figure 4A,B.

claim: Epi cells that do not undergo an EMT differentiate into neurectoderm, while those that undergo an EMT emanate from the PS and acquire mesoderm or DE identities.
source: Epi cells that do not undergo an EMT differentiate into neurectoderm, while those that undergo an EMT emanate from the PS and acquire mesoderm or DE identities (Arnold and Robertson, 2009; Ferrer-Vaquer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A PS-like population arose after 24 hr of in vitro differentiation followed by the formation of a 2–3 cell layer ridge at the colony perimeter at 48 hr.
source: A PS-like population arose after 24 hr of in vitro differentiation (Figure 2F) followed by the formation of a 2–3 cell layer ridge at the colony perimeter at 48 hr (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2F and Figure 4C,D.

claim: By 72 hr, the ridge was positioned more centrally, resulting in a volcano-like structure.
source: By 72 hr, the ridge was positioned more centrally, suggesting an inwards movement, resulting in a volcano-like structure (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4C,D.

claim: Cells at the border of the BRACHYURY-expressing region downregulated the epithelial marker CDH1 and upregulated the mesenchymal marker CDH2.
source: Cells at the border of the BRACHYURY-expressing region downregulated the epithelial marker CDH1 and upregulated the mesenchymal marker CDH2 (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The outer CDH2 expression domain correlated with the position of the PS (BRACHYURY), embryonic mesoderm (GATA6) and extraembryonic mesoderm (CDX2) populations.
source: As in vivo, the outer CDH2 expression domain correlated with the position of the PS (BRACHYURY), embryonic mesoderm (GATA6) and extraembryonic mesoderm (CDX2) populations (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4F.

claim: Both the intermediate PS-like domain and the outer embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm domain expressed SNAIL.
source: Furthermore, both the intermediate PS-like domain and the outer embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm domain expressed SNAIL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E), a transcriptional repressor that regulates the gastrulation EMT (Carver et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E and a citation.

claim: At 48 hr, CDH2-positive cells emerged at the base of the colony, beneath the CDH1-positive epithelial layer, and were observed more centrally over time.
source: At 48 hr, CDH2-positive cells emerged at the base of the colony, beneath the CDH1-positive epithelial layer, and were observed more centrally over time (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4D,E.

claim: BRACHYURY-expressing cells were occasionally observed in more central positions at 72 hr, which could suggest an inwards migration of mesenchymal PS derivatives between the upper epithelium and the surface of the micropattern slide.
source: We also occasionally observed BRACHYURY-expressing cells in more central positions at 72 hr (Figure 4F), which could suggest an inwards migration of mesenchymal PS derivatives between the upper epithelium and the surface of the micropattern slide.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Central posterior Epi-like cells maintained CDH1.
source: Conversely, central posterior Epi-like cells, maintained CDH1 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4D,E.

claim: Various signaling pathways including Wnt, FGF and TGFβ regulate EMT in development and cancer.
source: Various signaling pathways including Wnt, FGF and TGFβ regulate EMT in development and cancer (Ferrer-Vaquer et al., 2010; Kang and Massagué, 2004; Ciruna and Rossant, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The role of TGFβ signaling through SMAD2/3 in EMT has been well characterized.
source: In particular, the role of TGFβ signaling through SMAD2/3 has been well characterized (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mice with null mutations in Smad2/3 or Nodal do not gastrulate and lack normal mesoderm structures.
source: Mice with null mutations in Smad2/3 or Nodal do not gastrulate and lack normal mesoderm structures (Dunn et al., 2004; Nomura and Li, 1998; Weinstein et al., 1998; Conlon et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of Activin (Nodal) signaling, cells maintained high levels of CDH1 and accumulated at the edge of colonies.
source: In the absence of Activin (Nodal) signaling, cells maintained high levels of CDH1 and accumulated at the edge of colonies (Figure 4G,H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In the absence of Activin (Nodal) signaling, cells failed to downregulate SOX2 and did not differentiate, evidenced by the lack of BRACHYURY, GATA6, CDX2 or SOX17 expression.
source: Furthermore, they failed to downregulate SOX2 and did not differentiate, evidenced by the lack of BRACHYURY, GATA6, CDX2 or SOX17 expression (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In flat-disc-shaped micropatterns, SMAD2/3 signaling regulated the EMT associated with an exit from pluripotency and onset of differentiation.
source: Thus, in these flat-disc-shaped micropatterns, SMAD2/3 signaling regulated the EMT associated with an exit from pluripotency and onset of differentiation confirming that in vitro micropattern differentiation and in vivo gastrulation are regulated by common pathways and processes even though their geometries (flat-disc versus cup-shaped) are distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ACTIVIN inhibition experiment.

claim: In vitro micropattern differentiation and in vivo gastrulation are regulated by common pathways and processes even though their geometries (flat-disc versus cup-shaped) are distinct.
source: Thus, in these flat-disc-shaped micropatterns, SMAD2/3 signaling regulated the EMT associated with an exit from pluripotency and onset of differentiation confirming that in vitro micropattern differentiation and in vivo gastrulation are regulated by common pathways and processes even though their geometries (flat-disc versus cup-shaped) are distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of in vitro and in vivo systems.

claim: In the micropattern system, hESCs give rise to the broadest spectrum of cell fates when differentiated within colonies of 500–1000 μm diameter.
source: It was previously shown that, in the micropattern system, hESCs give rise to the broadest spectrum of cell fates when differentiated within colonies of 500–1000 μm diameter (Warmflash et al., 2014; Etoc et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on hESCs.

claim: When the micropattern diameter was decreased, the outer cell fate domains were preserved while the inner cell fates were lost, suggesting an edge-sensing input into the differentiation.
source: When the micropattern diameter was decreased, the outer cell fate domains were preserved while the inner cell fates were lost, suggesting an edge-sensing input into the differentiation (Warmflash et al., 2014; Etoc et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and represents an inference about edge-sensing.

claim: The temporal order of differentiation was maintained across the different colony diameters analyzed - 500, 225, 140 and 80 μm.
source: We noted that the temporal order of differentiation was maintained across the different colony diameters analyzed - 500, 225, 140 and 80 μm (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5C–E.

claim: The spatial organization of cell fates after 72 hr of differentiation was dependent on colony diameter.
source: However, the spatial organization of cell fates after 72 hr of differentiation was dependent on colony diameter (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5B summarizing the diameter-dependent patterns.

claim: Within 500 μm diameter colonies, the outer extraembryonic mesoderm population marked by CDX2 was maintained but BRACHYURY-positive PS cells were positioned within the colony center in place of the SOX2 only Epi-like population.
source: Within 500 μm diameter colonies, the outer extraembryonic mesoderm population marked by CDX2 was maintained but, in contrast to colonies of 1000 μm diameter, BRACHYURY-positive PS cells were positioned within the colony center in place of the SOX2 only Epi-like population (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At smaller micropattern diameters of 80–140 μm, colonies were comprised predominantly of CDX2 or SOX2 –positive cells with almost no BRACHYURY expression observed.
source: At even smaller micropattern diameters of 80–140 μm, colonies were comprised predominantly of CDX2 or SOX2 –positive cells with almost no BRACHYURY expression observed (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CDX2 and SOX2 marked distinct, apparently randomly positioned, clusters of cells in 80–140 μm diameter colonies.
source: CDX2 and SOX2 marked distinct, apparently randomly positioned, clusters of cells (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: On smaller diameter micropatterns, the width to height ratio of colonies was altered such that 80–140 μm diameter colonies generated taller, embryoid body-like aggregates.
source: It should be noted that, on smaller diameter micropatterns, the width to height ratio of colonies was altered such that 80–140 μm diameter colonies generated taller, embryoid body-like aggregates.
evidence: This is an observation about the morphology of smaller colonies.

claim: Over time, three-dimensional structures on smaller micropatterns exhibited morphological asymmetries, which may explain the loss of radial symmetry in marker expression.
source: Over time, these three-dimensional structures exhibited morphological asymmetries (Figure 5F), which may explain the loss of radial symmetry in marker expression.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Micropattern diameter is a critical factor in determining mouse PSC fate specification and patterning.
source: Taken together, these data show that micropattern diameter is a critical factor in determining mouse PSC fate specification and patterning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diameter experiments.

claim: The loss of central populations within 500 μm diameter colonies indicates that mouse PSCs may specify fates as a function of distance from the colony edge.
source: While the non-uniform, three-dimensional geometry of smaller colonies made data difficult to interpret, the loss of central populations within 500 μm diameter colonies indicates that, like human PSCs (Warmflash et al., 2014), mouse PSCs may specify fates as a function of distance from the colony edge.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter experiments and a citation to prior work on human PSCs.

claim: In E6.5-E6.75 embryos, BMP signaling (marked by pSMAD1/5/8) was active at low levels within the proximal, but not distal, Epi and elevated within cells of the PS and embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm.
source: In E6.5-E6.75 embryos, BMP signaling (marked by pSMAD1/5/8) was active at low levels within the proximal, but not distal, Epi and elevated within cells of the PS and embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing pSMAD1/5/8 staining.

claim: At E6.5-E6.75, pSMAD1/5/8 levels correlated with BRACHYURY expression.
source: At this stage, pSMAD1/5/8 levels correlated with BRACHYURY expression (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: From E7.0 onwards, as the PS extended, pSMAD1/5/8 was observed within the posterior PS but not anterior PS.
source: From E7.0 onwards, as the PS extended, pSMAD1/5/8 was observed within the posterior PS but not anterior PS, consistent with anterior cells being positioned furthest from the ExE source of BMP4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E and represents an inference about the source of BMP4.

claim: pSMAD1/5/8 was observed in embryonic Mesoderm 1 but not BRACHYURY-positive Mesoderm 2 cells.
source: Furthermore, pSMAD1/5/8 was observed in embryonic Mesoderm 1 but not BRACHYURY-positive Mesoderm 2 cells and consequently, the correlation with BRACHYURY expression was lost (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: At 0 hr of micropattern differentiation, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was observed at low levels throughout colonies, corresponding to the low BMP signaling activity within the proximal embryonic Epi at E6.5-E6.75.
source: At 0 hr of micropattern differentiation, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was observed at low levels throughout colonies (Figure 6C), corresponding to the low BMP signaling activity within the proximal embryonic Epi at E6.5-E6.75 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: From 24–72 hr of micropattern differentiation, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was elevated at the colony edge within the PS, embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm cell fate domains.
source: From 24–72 hr of micropattern differentiation, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was elevated at the colony edge within the PS, embryonic and extraembryonic mesoderm cell fate domains (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6C–E.

claim: At 24 and 48 hr, the majority of pSMAD1/5/8-positive cells expressed BRACHYURY but by 72 hr, the fraction of BRACHYURY/pSMAD1/5/8 -positive cells was significantly reduced.
source: At 24 and 48 hr, the majority of pSMAD1/5/8-positive cells expressed BRACHYURY but by 72 hr, the fraction of BRACHYURY/pSMAD1/5/8 -positive cells was significantly reduced (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: The reduction in BRACHYURY/pSMAD1/5/8 coexpression at 72 hr likely corresponded to the presence of nuclear pSMAD1/5/8, but not BRACHYURY, within Mesoderm 1 cells of the embryo.
source: This likely corresponded to the presence of nuclear pSMAD1/5/8, but not BRACHYURY, within Mesoderm 1 cells of the embryo (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison to in vivo data, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: As with micropattern differentiated hESCs, signaling activity exhibits radial dependence in mouse micropatterns.
source: These data revealed that, as with micropattern differentiated hESCs (Warmflash et al., 2014; Tewary et al., 2017; Etoc et al., 2016), signaling activity exhibits radial dependence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pSMAD1/5/8 data and citations to prior work on hESCs.

claim: The cell types identified within the in vitro micropattern system experienced a comparable BMP signaling history to their in vivo counterparts.
source: Furthermore, the cell types identified within the in vitro micropattern system experienced a comparable BMP signaling history to their in vivo counterparts, with low BMP signaling activity present within posterior Epi-like cells and elevated activity within the posterior PS, embryonic Mesoderm one and extraembryonic mesoderm populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of in vitro and in vivo BMP signaling patterns.

claim: In the presence of FGF, ACTIVIN, BMP and WNT, a signaling niche that lacked BMP activity, comparable to the distal Epi and anterior PS in vivo, was not observed within the micropatterned colonies.
source: In vivo, the distal Epi and anterior PS were devoid of BMP activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D,E) but, in the presence of FGF, ACTIVIN, BMP and WNT, a comparable signaling niche that lacked BMP activity was not observed within the micropatterned colonies.
evidence: This is an observation based on the comparison of in vitro and in vivo BMP signaling patterns, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D,E.

claim: The spatial organization of hESC-derived cell fates during micropattern differentiation is mediated by a combination of receptor occlusion at the colony center and loss of secreted inhibitors from the colony edge.
source: The spatial organization of hESC-derived cell fates during micropattern differentiation is mediated by a combination of receptor occlusion at the colony center and loss of secreted inhibitors from the colony edge (Tewary et al., 2017; Etoc et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on hESCs.

claim: When WNT3A was substituted with a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021, CDX2, GATA6 and SOX17 were expressed at the outer colony edge indicating that mesoderm differentiation was unaffected.
source: Under these conditions, CDX2, GATA6 and SOX17 were expressed at the outer colony edge indicating that mesoderm differentiation was unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: When WNT3A was substituted with CHIR99021, the BRACHYURY expression territory was expanded throughout the center of the colony.
source: However, the BRACHYURY expression territory was expanded throughout the center of the colony (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F), recapitulating the expansion of BRACHYURY expression in CHIR-cultured embryos (Sumi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F and a citation to prior work.

claim: The transmission of signals or activity of inhibitors through receptors is key for setting up distinct cell fate domains within the flat-disc micropatterned colonies.
source: These data suggest that the transmission of signals or activity of inhibitors through receptors is key for setting up distinct cell fate domains within the flat-disc micropatterned colonies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CHIR experiment.

claim: In +BMP conditions, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was observed in cells at the perimeter of colonies alongside CDX2 and SOX17, followed by a region of BRACHYURY expression and a central region of cells expressing SOX2 and low levels of FOXA2.
source: In +BMP conditions, nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 was observed in cells at the perimeter of colonies alongside CDX2 and SOX17, followed by a region of BRACHYURY expression and a central region of cells expressing SOX2 and low levels of FOXA2 (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7B–E.

claim: In medium conditions lacking BMP (-BMP), the absence of BMP signaling activity was confirmed by lack of nuclear pSMAD1/5/8.
source: In medium conditions lacking BMP (-BMP), the absence of BMP signaling activity was confirmed by lack of nuclear pSMAD1/5/8 (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7B,E.

claim: Under -BMP conditions, the domain of extraembryonic mesoderm, marked by CDX2, was lost.
source: Under these conditions, the domain of extraembryonic mesoderm, marked by CDX2, was lost (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7C,E.

claim: Under -BMP conditions, elevated SOX17 in outer cells was robustly coexpressed with FOXA2, representing DE.
source: Instead we observed elevated SOX17 in outer cells, which was now robustly coexpressed with FOXA2 (Figure 7D–F) representing DE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Under -BMP conditions, a separate population of outer cells coexpressed FOXA2 and BRACHYURY, likely representing cells within the anterior PS, node or AxM.
source: We also observed a separate population of outer cells that coexpressed FOXA2 and BRACHYURY (Figure 7F,G), likely representing cells within the anterior PS, node or AxM (Figure 3A, yellow arrowheads,Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression patterns, supported by Figure 7F,G, Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In the absence of BMP, FOXA2, BRACHYURY and GscGFP expression was observed at the edge of micropatterned colonies from 24 hr of differentiation, followed by HhexRedStar expression at 48 hr.
source: In the absence of BMP, we observed FOXA2, BRACHYURY and GscGFP expression at the edge of micropatterned colonies from 24 hr of differentiation, followed by HhexRedStar expression at 48 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The majority of HhexRedStar-positive cells coexpressed GscGFP and FOXA2, a signature of both DE and AxM.
source: The majority of HhexRedStar-positive cells coexpressed GscGFP and FOXA2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E) a signature of both DE and AxM.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Little overlap was observed between GscGFP, HhexRedStar and the AxM marker BRACHYURY within individual cells, hence GscGFP/HhexRedStar/FOXA2 coexpression likely represented DE.
source: However, as we observed little overlap between GscGFP, HhexRedStar and the AxM marker BRACHYURY within individual cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G), GscGFP/HhexRedStar/FOXA2 coexpression likely represented DE.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker coexpression patterns, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: The FOXA2/BRACHYURY-coexpressing cells observed in the absence of BMP may correspond to a subpopulation of anterior PS cells or alternatively AxM cells that have downregulated Gsc and Hhex.
source: The FOXA2/BRACHYURY-coexpressing cells observed in the absence of BMP (Figure 7F,G) may correspond to a subpopulation of anterior PS cells (Figure 3A) or alternatively AxM cells that have downregulated Gsc and Hhex.
evidence: This is a speculation about the identity of these cells, supported by Figure 7F,G and Figure 3A.

claim: Cells that coexpressed GscGFP and FOXA2 but not HhexRedStar were frequently observed, which may represent a BRACHYURY negative anterior PS-like state.
source: We also frequently observed cells that coexpressed GscGFP and FOXA2 but not HhexRedStar (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), which may represent a BRACHYURY negative anterior PS-like state (Figure 3A) (Burtscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about the identity of these cells, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3A and a citation.

claim: In conditions lacking BMP signaling activity, SOX2 levels were elevated relative to those in the presence of BMP, suggesting that central cells represent a more anterior Epi state.
source: In conditions lacking BMP signaling activity, SOX2 levels were elevated relative to those in the presence of BMP (Figure 7B–E). This suggested that central cells represent a more anterior Epi state.
evidence: This is an inference based on SOX2 levels, supported by Figure 7B–E.

claim: In the absence of BMP, Sox1GFP was expressed at high levels throughout the colony center.
